cards.prompt: Import matplotlib's plotting module under the usual alias.
cards.why: matplotlib is the whole library; pyplot is the module you actually call. Everyone aliases it plt, so matching that makes your code readable to anyone.
cards.whenToUse: The first line of any matplotlib work.
cards.commonMistake: Writing `import matplotlib as plt`, which imports the package but not the plotting functions, so plt.subplots() fails.

cards.prompt: Make a figure and one axes, then draw a pandas bar chart onto that axes.
cards.why: plt.subplots() returns two things: the figure (the whole canvas) and the axes (the plot area you draw on). Passing ax= to pandas is what lets you keep control of the layout.
cards.whenToUse: Any time you need more than one plot, or want to touch the axes afterwards.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting that subplots() returns a *pair*. Writing `ax = plt.subplots()` gives you a tuple, and every ax.something call then fails.

cards.prompt: Draw bars straight onto the axes from two plain lists: the labels and the heights.
cards.why: The axes methods take raw sequences, not a DataFrame. That is the trade: more typing than pandas, but it works on any data and you control every piece.
cards.whenToUse: Data that isn't in a DataFrame, or a chart pandas can't express.
cards.commonMistake: Passing a DataFrame to ax.bar(). It wants the x values and the heights as separate sequences.

cards.prompt: Head the axes with "Revenue per region" and label the y-axis "revenue".
cards.answer:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(['East', 'North', 'West'], [225, 115, 245])
ax.set_title('Revenue per region')
ax.set_ylabel('revenue')
cards.why: In the object-oriented style every label is a setter on the axes: set_title, set_xlabel, set_ylabel. The pattern is regular, so once you know one you know them all.
cards.whenToUse: Every chart anyone else will read.
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for ax.title = '…'. These are methods, not attributes, so assignment silently replaces the artist instead of setting the text.
cards.starterCode:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(['East', 'North', 'West'], [225, 115, 245])
ax.___('Revenue per region')
ax.set_ylabel('revenue')

cards.why: Drawing straight onto an axes means nothing is labelled for you — unlike pandas, which names the x-axis from the index. Every label is yours to set.
cards.whenToUse: Whenever the axis quantity isn't obvious from the tick labels alone.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming matplotlib will infer labels the way pandas does. It has no column names to work from.

cards.prompt: Force the y-axis to run from 0 to 300 rather than auto-scaling.
cards.why: Auto-scaling picks a range from the data, which means two charts of the same thing can end up with different axes and look falsely different. Pinning the limits makes charts comparable.
cards.whenToUse: Comparing charts side by side, or forcing a bar chart to start at zero.
cards.commonMistake: Publishing two charts with auto-scaled axes and comparing their bar heights by eye — the scales don't match, so the comparison is meaningless.

cards.prompt: Draw a line through five revenue values on the axes.
cards.why: Given one sequence, ax.plot() treats it as the y values and uses 0, 1, 2… for x. Pass two sequences and the first becomes x.
cards.whenToUse: A quick line where the position in the list is the x-axis.
cards.commonMistake: Expecting ax.plot(y) to invent meaningful x values. The x-axis is just the index.

cards.prompt: Scatter revenue against units, passing the two columns straight in.
cards.why: The axes methods happily take pandas Series — they are sequences of numbers, which is all matplotlib asks for. x comes first, y second.
cards.whenToUse: A scatter where you want full control of the axes afterwards.
cards.commonMistake: Passing y before x. There are no keyword names to save you here; order is the contract.

cards.prompt: Bucket revenue into 4 bins and chart how many rows land in each.
cards.why: ax.hist() does the bucketing itself, so it takes the raw values — not counts. The bars it draws are frequencies.
cards.whenToUse: Checking the shape of a distribution.
cards.commonMistake: Counting the values yourself first and then calling hist(), which buckets your counts instead of your data.

cards.prompt: Draw the same region totals as horizontal bars.
cards.why: ax.barh() takes the categories first and the lengths second, the same argument order as ax.bar() — only the direction changes.
cards.commonMistake: Swapping the arguments because the bars now run along x. The category sequence still comes first.

cards.prompt: Draw two lines on one axes and show the key that names them.
cards.answer:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([120, 95, 80], label='West')
ax.plot([60, 70, 65], label='East')
ax.legend()
cards.why: Calling plot twice on the same axes layers both lines. Each takes its own label=, but nothing appears until ax.legend() asks matplotlib to collect them.
cards.whenToUse: Two comparable series that share a scale.
cards.commonMistake: Setting label= and expecting a legend. Without ax.legend() the labels exist but are never drawn.
cards.starterCode:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([120, 95, 80], label='West')
ax.plot([60, 70, 65], label='East')
ax.___()

cards.prompt: Put revenue and units side by side per region by offsetting each set of bars, then name the ticks.
cards.answer:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
x = np.arange(3)
ax.bar(x - 0.2, [225, 115, 245], width=0.4, label='revenue')
ax.bar(x + 0.2, [22, 11, 25], width=0.4, label='units')
ax.set_xticks(x, ['East', 'North', 'West'])
ax.legend()
cards.why: matplotlib has no 'grouped bar' function — you place them yourself. Bars sit at numeric positions, so you shift one set left and one right by half a bar, then relabel the ticks with names.
cards.whenToUse: Grouped bars where pandas or seaborn isn't available or doesn't fit.
cards.commonMistake: Offsetting the bars but forgetting set_xticks, leaving 0, 1, 2 on the axis instead of the category names.
cards.starterCode:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
x = np.arange(3)
ax.bar(x - 0.2, [225, 115, 245], width=0.4, label='revenue')
ax.bar(x + 0.2, [22, 11, 25], width=0.4, label='units')
ax.___(x, ['East', 'North', 'West'])
ax.legend()

cards.prompt: Make one row of two plots and draw a different bar chart in each.
cards.why: subplots(rows, cols) hands back an array of axes instead of one. You index into it and draw on each panel independently.
cards.whenToUse: Several related charts that belong in one figure.
cards.commonMistake: Treating the returned array as a single axes. With more than one panel you must index it — axes[0], not axes.

cards.prompt: Two panels that must be compared — make them share one y-axis.
cards.answer:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, sharey=True)
axes[0].bar(['Bags', 'Shoes'], [125, 120])
axes[1].bar(['Bags', 'Shoes'], [60, 165])
cards.why: By default every panel scales itself, so a small panel's bars can look as tall as a big panel's. sharey=True puts them all on one scale, which is what makes side-by-side panels honest.
cards.whenToUse: Any set of panels a reader will compare — which is almost always.
cards.commonMistake: Leaving panels independently scaled and concluding two groups are similar when one axis tops out at 165 and the other at 300.

cards.prompt: Make a 2×2 grid and loop over every panel in one pass.
cards.why: A 2D grid gives you a 2D array, so axes[0][1] works but looping needs two loops. .flat flattens it to a single sequence you can iterate once.
cards.whenToUse: Drawing the same kind of chart into every cell of a grid.
cards.commonMistake: Looping over `axes` directly on a 2D grid, which yields whole *rows* of axes rather than individual ones.

cards.prompt: Plot without making a figure first, then reach for the axes matplotlib created implicitly and title it.
cards.why: plt.plot() draws onto a 'current' figure it creates for you, and plt.gca() — get current axes — hands that axes back. It is convenient in a notebook and a liability in a script, where 'current' is easy to lose track of.
cards.whenToUse: Quick throwaway plots. Prefer fig, ax = plt.subplots() for anything you'll maintain.
cards.commonMistake: Mixing the two styles in one script, so plt.title() lands on whichever axes happens to be current rather than the one you meant.

cards.prompt: You already have `ax`. Which call titles that one axes, in the object-oriented style?
cards.why: The axes owns its own title, and ax.set_title names it directly. fig.suptitle heads the whole figure — a different thing that sits above every panel — and plt.title works only on whatever axes is 'current'.
cards.whenToUse: Titling one panel among several, where 'current axes' is ambiguous.
cards.commonMistake: Using fig.suptitle for a single-panel figure. It works, but it sits higher and detaches from the plot, and it titles every panel once you add more.

cards.prompt: Which call drew these two panels?
cards.answer:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, sharey=True)
axes[0].bar(['Bags', 'Shoes'], [125, 120])
axes[1].bar(['Bags', 'Shoes'], [60, 165])
cards.why: Two panels in a row means subplots(1, 2). The giveaway for sharey is the right panel: its bars reach higher than the left panel's, which only happens when both are measured against one scale.
cards.whenToUse: Judging whether panels you're shown are safe to compare.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming panels share a scale. Unless sharey was passed, each one auto-scales and the heights aren't comparable.
distractors:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharey=True)
axes[0].bar(['Bags', 'Shoes'], [125, 120])
axes[1].bar(['Bags', 'Shoes'], [60, 165])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, sharey=True)
axes[0].bar(['Bags', 'Shoes'], [60, 165])
axes[1].bar(['Bags', 'Shoes'], [125, 120])

cards.why: Bars running left to right off a named axis means barh, and the categories are in the order they were passed — East, North, West — not sorted by length.
cards.whenToUse: Reading a chart back to the axes method that drew it.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming the bars were sorted. matplotlib draws them in the order given; here the longest is last.
